narrative:
It was a rare (lately) 5 golf ball day today with warm and dry conditions. The evening is pleasant but clouds increase overnight and Thursday with chances of rain in the morning and later in the afternoon. Friday still looks to be a mostly cloudy, showery and damp day with cooler temperatures. Temperatures continue to be pleasant over the weekend but a few showers and storms may pop on Saturday. Sunday looks dry though.

The Monday Message is available to subscribers. Can we finally sneak-in a rain-free midweek?

Aug 10, 2026 July 2026 Recap Holiday Heatwave At the start of the month, there was no relief in sight for the continued dry conditions that the region has been experiencing dating back to the final few months of 2025. July arrived ready to make things worse with what will almost certainly be the heatwave of record for 2026, as record highs abounded throughout the Southern Appalachians for the first handful of days in the month. It felt fitting that America's 250th birthday would coincide with one of the hottest July 4ths on record. Mother Nature seemed to want to celebrate with a bang along with the rest of us. We already wrote extensively about this heatwave a few weeks ago, so if you'd like the full recap, click this link. The quick & dirty version: upper-level ridging and surface high pressure settled over our region, delivering 100s to the Foothills, 90s to the mountains, and 80s to the high elevations. The table below shows recorded highs vs the previous record for each day, with new records highlighted in red, and ties in yellow. Jefferson's 4 consecutive 90F+ highs were all records from the 2nd to the 5th. Beech Mountain does not have an especially long period of record (less than 40 years), but 85F on the 4th is the new highest temperature recorded during that period. The hottest temperatures recorded on our Ray's Weather network of stations throughout this heatwave: 103.0F at Roaring River, 7/3 102.3F at Lenoir, 7/2 102.2F at Morganton-Lenoir Airport, 7/2 & 7/3 100.8F at Hickory, 7/2 96.3F at Asheville, 7/2 93.0F at Boone, 7/2 79.9F at Mount Mitchell, 7/2 (the all-time record is 81F!) Things settled back into a more normal summertime rythym after the heat, with afternoon thunderstorms kicking back up and delivering scattered downpours that began to help some recover their annual rainfall deficit. We'll get deeper into the heavy rains that many experienced in the month of July later on, but the daily graph below shows the story for Celo. Right after the heatwave, over 5 inches of rain fell from the 5th through the 12th, which is pretty close to the average rainfall for the entire month there. One of six days with over an inch of rain in Celo was an abnormally cool July 13th, when 1.47" fell at the foot of the Black Mountains. Further north, stationary showers would make that number pale in comparison. Roaring Gap's Record Rain On the 13th, a cool-air wedge was in place along the eastern side of the Appalachians, and rain showers abounded as moist air was lifted and condensed over the cooler air at the surface. Hickory picked up nearly 2 inches of rain, one of the wettest days of the month there. Along the Eastern Escarpment (an explainer if you need a refresher on the local geography), near where Alleghany, Wilkes, and Surry counties meet, our station at Roaring Gap recorded over 9 inches of rain! Radar estimates nearby exceed 10 inches, and flooding was reported in the area. 9 inches of rain in less than 24 hours will produce flooding anywhere, but fairly dry antecedent conditions likely aided in flooding not being as bad as it could have been. To get such an incredible one-day total, you usually need the help of terrain - which we had in this case. A steady supply of moist air moving up the slope of the escarpment region with little to no "steering" flow to move things around produces stationary showers that can drop localized buckets of rain. A short drive to Mount Airy or eastern Ashe County would have decreased your rainfall amounts as much as tenfold that day! This incredible event, combined with a generally quite wet July, produced a whopping 14.22 inches of rain at Roaing Gap for the month. We'll get into the specifics in the "Precipitation" section further on. A Rare Mountain Tornado A cold front in the summertime usually does not pack much punch, unlike the cold season fronts that put snowflakes and a bitter chill to the air. However, the month of July ended with a couple of abnormally cool mornings, with 40s in the High Country on the 30th. For such an impressive cooldown, you need to bring in a fairly stout front by summer standards, and when you do that, sparks fly. Summer heat and humidity is a powder-keg for storms, and a front adds a focal point to produce more vigorous activity. We got plenty of activity on the 28th! Up in Madison County, just the fifth tornado ever officially surveyed in the county occurred at 5:51PM. It was a weak EF0 tornado, with winds estimated near 80 mph. The track was just 1.1 miles, and the width of the tornado was 75 yards at its widest. The small blue line shows the track below. Damage was "minor and sporadic," limited to broken branches along with a few uprooted and snapped trees. Oddly enough, while there are only 5 surveyed tornadoes on record for Madison Co, 3 of them occurred this year (with two on March 16th). Even outside of the tornado itself, trees were knocked down throughout the county and power outages were common thanks to strong straight-line winds. Our station at Woodson Branch Nature School about 8 or 9 miles northwest of Marshall recorded 2.24 inches of rain before dropping out due to power & internet issues. Temperatures High temperatures were largely fairly close to normal (generally just above it) through the month, with the exceptions being the remarkable heat around the 4th and a couple of cool-air wedge events centered around the 13th and 24th. Those wedges weren't enough for most locations, as highs wound up above normal for most. More of a difference was made in low temperatures, as all of the stations included in the table below were above normal to well above normal on lows. This is thanks to the incredibly humid month we experienced, as moisture and cloud cover do not allow temperatures to drop very much overnight. As a result, it was an above average temperature month region-wide. Specifics lie in the table and map below.

Precipitation July 2026 was about as wet as can be for most. The "percent of normal precip" column does not tell the story as well as the total numbers and the days with precip. Many locations had rain on half or more of the days in July. Celo, Edgemont, Blowing Rock, and Roaring Gap all recorded over 10 inches of rain for the month! Remove Blowing Rock from the grouping, and those 3 stations picked up more than a foot. The vast majority of our stations recieved more than their average rainfall, aside from a few exceptions - notably Jefferson, which the map below the table shows well. Ashe County did not have the rainfall luck that many others did in July. Of the ~60 stations that did not experience outages during July, 38 recorded over 6 inches of rain for the month, and 17 recorded over 8 inches. Amazingly, the area was far enough behind on precipitation for 2026 that techincally, drought conditions do persist for most. However, the level of drought has been reduced notably. But Boone did remained roughly 8 inches "behind schedule" at the end of July (reduced to about 5 inches thanks to heavy rains to start August).
